Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

vignette: Arjun Patel had never imagined the scuffed ceiling tiles of his bedroom would become the permanent backdrop of his worst moments. Six months ago, during a sharp exchange over misplaced keys and unreturned calls, his then-partner had lunged across the narrow hallway. The struggle was sudden and entirely physical—a heavy palm pressing flat against his sternum, the firm grip of a forearm across his throat, and the hard thud of his shoulder against the sideboard. What stayed with him was not merely the bruising, but the wet heat of his partner’s sweat rising between them, the specific cadence of the shouting that spiraled into certain words he still recognizes as triggers: careless, always, why won’t you. The event was not drawn out, but it was precise enough to leave the world feeling permanently tilted. In the weeks that followed, Arjun found his body keeping time as if the struggle were still unfolding. When regular customers in his downtown grocery shop wiped their foreheads or leaned in to inspect his stock, the familiar scent of sweat and body odour would catch in the warm air, and he would feel a sharp, familiar tightness across his own chest. He had come to believe that the atmosphere itself carried the weight of that night. Conversation topics began to matter as much as smells. A supplier asking about his living situation, or a neighbor mentioning a recent breakup, would send the memory of the event tumbling into his mind without warning. Sometimes it arrived with a clear picture—the sideboard, the narrow hallway, the press of the hand. Other times, the image dissolved entirely, leaving only the full emotional intensity, a quiet but overwhelming current of dread and a sudden flare of rage when he recalled exactly how he had stood still, letting the grip hold him down. He would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. Days passed with a manageable rhythm, but nights grew heavy. Arjun found it harder to feel safe after the streetlights came on. The quiet of the shop after closing made the aisles feel exposed, and he would lie awake, listening to the hum of the refrigeration units, certain that a stranger’s approach in the ordinary daytime counter was just as threatening as any sudden movement in the dark. He was not sure he could rely on himself to read the room correctly, and this uncertainty settled alongside his growing habits. He started keeping the back door chained during evening deliveries, and he began closing the front register an hour early on busy Saturdays. At home, his current partner noticed how he flinched when hands reached toward him, how he paced the small kitchen while the evening news played, unable to settle into sleep. His body kept reacting to phantom pressure, even when the room was still. The accumulated weight of these shifts finally crossed a threshold last month. A regular customer, wiping sweat from his brow while discussing the price of cardamom, asked Arjun a simple question about his partner. The topic struck him like a physical prompt, and the memory returned fully, accompanied by that familiar surge of rage. Arjun realized he had begun avoiding the very people and conversations that sustained his livelihood, shrinking his shop’s hours and retreating from weekend plans to keep the noise and the approaching figures at bay. A PCL-5 score of 80 captured the steady alarm that now defined his days. He had come to believe that if he let his guard down, the old grip would return, and he would be helpless again. Now, sitting in a therapist’s office with his hands resting carefully on his knees, Arjun hopes to find a way to trust his own reactions again. He is most afraid of waking to the same silent threat, but he is ready to stay awake long enough to untangle the scent, the sound, and the guilt that have settled into his days.
